title: VoMP: Predicting Volumetric Mechanical Property Fields
claim: One feed-forward model quickly predicts physically meaningful property fields for varied 3D representations, enabling realistic downstream simulation.
layout: 2 columns, each with input→output on top and simulation frames below
description: The figure has two side-by-side columns, each with a top row and a bottom row. On the left, a black mesh of a sofa chair goes through a green "VoMP" arrow labeled 8s. It produces three voxelized chairs colored by Young's Modulus, Poisson's Ratio and Density, each with a viridis colorbar. Orange annotations point to materials such as metal, leather cushion and bedframe. On the right, a 3D Gaussian Splat ficus plant goes through a "VoMP" arrow labeled 3s. It produces three voxelized plants with the same three property maps, and the callout "Realistic Material Values" points to leaves, concrete and dirt. The bottom row shows simulation frames in rounded boxes: a bowling ball falling on a bed (orange box) and 65 ficuses falling into a container (green box). The eye goes first to the green arrows and the colorful voxel fields.
caption: VoMP predicts physically accurate volumetric mechanical property fields across 3D representations in just a few seconds (top), enabling their use in realistic deformable simulations (bottom).
abstract: Physical simulation relies on spatially-varying mechanical properties, often laboriously hand-crafted. VoMP is a feed-forward method trained to predict Young's modulus ($E$), Poisson's ratio ($Î½$), and density ($Ï$) throughout the volume of 3D objects, in any representation that can be rendered and voxelized. VoMP aggregates per-voxel multi-view features and passes them to our trained Geometry Transformer to predict per-voxel material latent codes. These latents reside on a manifold of physically plausible materials, which we learn from a real-world dataset, guaranteeing the validity of decoded per-voxel materials. To obtain object-level training data, we propose an annotation pipeline combining knowledge from segmented 3D datasets, material databases, and a vision-language model, along with a new benchmark. Experiments show that VoMP estimates accurate volumetric properties, far outperforming prior art in accuracy and speed.
